Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           In this breach of contract dispute, defendant Fidelity Information Services, LLC, d/b/a

                                  14   Atelio (“Atelio”) moves to stay this proceeding and compel plaintiff NerdWallet, Inc.

                                  15   (“NerdWallet”) into arbitration, as the parties’ original contract contains an arbitration clause.

                                  16   NerdWallet disagrees. In its view, the language of this clause suggests that arbitration is

                                  17   permissive, not mandatory. NerdWallet is mistaken. While the arbitration provision includes

                                  18   language that can be interpreted as permissive, the overall structure and context of the contract

                                  19   confirms that the purpose of the clause was to mandate arbitration upon a party’s request. Atelio’s

                                  20   motion to stay and compel arbitration is GRANTED. Its request for attorneys’ fees to cover the

                                  21   costs of litigating this dispute is DENIED because NerdWallet did not advocate for its

                                  22   interpretation of the contract in bad faith.

                                  23                                              BACKGROUND

                                  24   I.      Nerdwallet’s Allegations
                                  25           NerdWallet is a “leading personal finance company incorporated in the state of Delaware

                                  26   and with its principal place of business in San Mateo, California.” Complaint (“Compl.”) [Dkt.

                                  27   No. 1] ¶ 10. Atelio is a financial technology company and is a “wholly owned subsidiary of

                                  28   Fidelity National Information Services, Inc., a Fortune 500 company that bills itself as a leading
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO            Document 36         Filed 03/11/26    Page 2 of 13




                                   1   global provider of financial technology solutions.” Id. ¶¶ 11–12.

                                   2          In June 2023, NerdWallet began engaging with Atelio to “provide certain services in

                                   3   connection with the NerdUp card,” a tool that would “allow[] users to build credit with minimal

                                   4   risk by depositing funds in an account and using those funds to cover their future NerdUp Card

                                   5   purchases.” Id. ¶¶ 13–14. The parties executed a Terms of Use agreement, which gave Atelio

                                   6   “primary responsibility for most aspects of the NerdUp Card’s operations,” including “issuing

                                   7   cards,” “creating and maintaining an online application for customers,” and “handling collection

                                   8   activities on past due-accounts,” amongst other things. Id. ¶¶ 15–16. Atelio also agreed to “use

                                   9   commercially reasonable efforts to address customer issues and assist NerdWallet during [its]

                                  10   wind-down process.” Id. ¶ 17.

                                  11          In late 2024, NerdWallet decided to discontinue its NerdUp Card. Id. ¶ 19. As a result, the

                                  12   parties executed an Addendum to the Terms of Use on November 22, 2024, “reiterating their
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   commitment to cooperate on the closure of the program and agreeing to effectuate a ‘Wind-Down

                                  14   Plan.’” Id. According to NerdWallet, the wind-down of the NerdUp Card was “not a complex

                                  15   undertaking,” and Atelio only had a few responsibilities, including to “[d]isable NerdUp Cards,

                                  16   and prevent further deposits or withdrawals, on the ‘freeze date’ of February 17, 2025”; “[i]ssue

                                  17   refund checks to customers who did not withdraw their funds before the freeze date”; “[r]equest

                                  18   NerdWallet’s cooperation ‘in a timely manner’ if such cooperation was needed to effectuate

                                  19   refunds”; “[d]eliver final statements to users”; and “[c]omplete its wind-down obligations by an

                                  20   agreed April2 1, 2025 Closure Date.” Id. ¶ 20.

                                  21          “Put mildly,” NerdWallet alleges, “Atelio’s performance [of the Wind-Down Plan] has

                                  22   been a disaster.” Id. ¶ 23. NerdWallet maintains that Atelio has failed to “timely issue refunds” to

                                  23   over 1,600 NerdUp customers on the freeze date. Id. ¶¶ 24–25. While it indicated to NerdWallet

                                  24   that the “entire refund process would be completed by the end of March 2025,” Atelio “did not

                                  25   send out a single check until April 14, 2025.” Id. ¶ 26. This meant that numerous NerdUp

                                  26   customers never received refunds until after the refund process was scheduled to be completed.

                                  27   See id. “Nearly five months after the freeze date, the refund process still ha[d] not been

                                  28   completed, in plain breach of Atelio’s obligation to timely issue refund checks.” Id. ¶ 28.
                                                                                         2
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO            Document 36          Filed 03/11/26     Page 3 of 13




                                   1          Moreover, NerdWallet asserts that many customers who did receive checks from Atelio

                                   2   were “unable to access their funds because the checks they received were rejected by their banks.”

                                   3   Id. ¶ 29. Atelio “never notified NerdWallet that it had issued invalid checks.” Id. ¶ 30. Instead, it

                                   4   “discovered the issue after customers began complaining in April 2025.” Id. Similarly, Atelio

                                   5   allegedly failed to calculate the statement balances for “at least five customers,” yet failed to

                                   6   communicate with these customers for “more than a month because Atelio initially provided

                                   7   NerdWallet with incorrect user IDs.” Id. ¶ 40. Put together, NerdWallet asserts that Atelio failed

                                   8   to live up to the requirements in the Terms of Use and Addendum, as Atelio did not “reasonably

                                   9   assist NerdWallet” with the Wind-Down process. Id. ¶ 33. Nor did Atelio “timely notify

                                  10   NerdWallet of issues with the refund process,” instead choosing to “ke[ep] NerdWallet in the dark

                                  11   about numerous key issues.” Id. ¶ 34.

                                  12   II.    Procedural History
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          On September 25, 2025, NerdWallet filed this action, raising claims for breach of contract

                                  14   and indemnification. See id. ¶¶ 51–60. Atelio then moved to compel arbitration and for costs

                                  15   associated with filing its motion on December 19, 2025. See Defendant Fidelity Information

                                  16   Services, LLC’s Notice of Motion (“Mot.”) [Dkt. No. 20]. NerdWallet filed its opposition on

                                  17   January 1, 2026. See NerdWallet, Inc.’s Opposition to Defendant Fidelity Information Services,

                                  18   LLC’s Motion to Stay and Compel Arbitration (“Oppo.”) [Dkt. No. 30]. Atelio replied on January

                                  19   23, 2025. See Defendant Fidelity Information Services, LLC’s Reply in Support of Motion to

                                  20   Stay and Compel Arbitration and for Costs (“Repl.”) [Dkt. No. 33]. I heard oral argument on

                                  21   March 4, 2026.

                                  22                                          LEGAL STANDARD

                                  23          The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”) governs the motion to compel arbitration. 9 U.S.C.

                                  24   §§ 1 et seq. Under the FAA, a district court determines: (i) whether a valid agreement to arbitrate

                                  25   exists and, if it does, (ii) whether the agreement encompasses the dispute at issue. Lifescan, Inc. v.

                                  26   Premier Diabetic Servs., Inc., 363 F.3d 1010, 1012 (9th Cir. 2004). “To evaluate the validity of

                                  27   an arbitration agreement, federal courts should apply ordinary state-law principles that govern the

                                  28   formation of contracts.” Ingle v. Circuit City Stores, Inc., 328 F.3d 1165, 1170 (9th Cir. 2003)
                                                                                          3
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO            Document 36          Filed 03/11/26     Page 4 of 13




                                   1   (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).

                                   2          If the court is satisfied “that the making of the arbitration agreement or the failure to

                                   3   comply with the agreement is not in issue, the court shall make an order directing the parties to

                                   4   proceed to arbitration in accordance with the terms of the agreement.” 9 U.S.C. § 4. “Any doubts

                                   5   concerning the scope of arbitrable issues should be resolved in favor of arbitration.” Simula, Inc.

                                   6   v. Autoliv, Inc., 175 F.3d 716, 719 (9th Cir. 1999).

                                   7                                              DISCUSSION

                                   8   I.     Motion to Stay and Compel Arbitration
                                   9          Neither party disputes that the first prong of the arbitration analysis—whether a valid

                                  10   agreement to arbitrate exists—is met. Both parties acknowledge the Terms of Use as controlling

                                  11   authority. It is also clear that the arbitration agreement covers this dispute if applied. See

                                  12   Lifescan, Inc., 363 F.3d at 1012. What remains in dispute, therefore, is whether the arbitration
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   clause is mandatory or permissive. I first address the parties’ concerns regarding whether public

                                  14   policy requires me to favor arbitration over reading the agreement using principles of contract

                                  15   interpretation (it does not). I then address the merits of the parties’ motions, ultimately finding

                                  16   that the arbitration provision is mandatory.

                                  17          a.      Whether Public Policy Supports Enforcement of the Arbitration Provision
                                  18          Atelio first asserts that the FAA compels me to enforce the parties’ arbitration agreement.

                                  19   See Mot. at 11–15. Under 9 U.S.C. § 2, arbitration agreements generally “shall be valid,

                                  20   irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation

                                  21   of any contract.” Similarly, under 9 U.S.C. § 3, courts are required to stay litigation of arbitral

                                  22   claims “in accordance with the terms of the agreement.” “The principal purpose of the FAA is to

                                  23   ensur[e] that private arbitration agreements are enforced according to their terms.” AT&T Mobility

                                  24   LLC v. Concepcion, 563 U.S. 333, 344 (2011) (internal quotation marks omitted).

                                  25          Atelio maintains that the United States Supreme Court has “recognized . . . strong public

                                  26   policy in favor of arbitration.” See Mot. at 12–13 (collecting cases). NerdWallet points out that

                                  27   two recent appellate decisions show that this policy no longer exists. Oppo. at 4. First, in Morgan

                                  28   v. Sundance, Inc., the Supreme Court considered whether the FAA authorized defendants to
                                                                                          4
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO             Document 36           Filed 03/11/26   Page 5 of 13




                                   1   invoke an arbitration clause after the parties litigated the cases for an extended period of time,

                                   2   including “filing motions to dismiss, answering complaints, and discussing settlement.” 596 U.S.

                                   3   411, 413 (2022). Prior to Morgan, many circuits applied a rule of waiver specific to arbitration,

                                   4   finding that a party could “waive its arbitration right by litigating only when its conduct has

                                   5   prejudiced the other side.” Id. at 413–14 (emphasis added). Most justified this rule based on the

                                   6   FAA’s “policy favoring arbitration.” See id. The Court disagreed. While it acknowledged the

                                   7   existence of a “policy favoring arbitration,” it emphasized that courts may not use the FAA to

                                   8   “invent special, arbitration-preferring procedural rules.” See id. at 418 (quoting Mohes H. Cone

                                   9   Memorial Hospital v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 24 (1983)). Rather, courts should

                                  10   understand “arbitration agreements as enforceable as other contracts, but not more so.” Morgan,

                                  11   596 U.S. at 418 (quoting Prima Paint Corp. v. Flood & Conklin Mfg. Co., 388 U.S. 395, 404 n.12

                                  12   (1967)). In other words, the FAA requires courts to “treat[] arbitration contracts like all others,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   not . . . foster[] arbitration.” Id. (emphasis added).

                                  14           Later, in Armstrong v. Michaels Stores, Inc., a Ninth Circuit panel applied Morgan and

                                  15   considered the circuit’s own treatment of arbitration agreements. 59 F.4th 1011, 1013 (9th Cir.

                                  16   2023). While the plaintiff in Armstrong originally agreed to arbitrate “any disputes regarding the

                                  17   terms and conditions of her employment,” a dispute arose that resulted in plaintiff filing the

                                  18   lawsuit. Id. The district court ordered the plaintiff to take her claim to arbitration. Id. She then

                                  19   appealed, arguing the defendant “waited too long to move for arbitration and therefore waived its

                                  20   right to the arbitral forum.” Id. The Ninth Circuit panel affirmed the district court, noting that the

                                  21   defendant “repeatedly reserved its right to arbitration, did not ask the district court to weigh in on

                                  22   the merits, and did not engage in any meaningful discovery.” Id. “Indeed,” the court found, “the

                                  23   only significant motion filed was [defendant’s] motion to compel arbitration.” Id. And while

                                  24   defendant did not immediately move to compel arbitration, the court found that “its actions d[id]

                                  25   not amount to a relinquishment of the right to arbitrate.” Id.

                                  26           Taken together, Morgan and Armstrong show that courts cannot favor arbitration

                                  27   agreements as compared to other contractual arrangements. See, e.g., Jackson v. Amazon.com,

                                  28   Inc., 65 F.4th 1093, 1105 n.1 (9th Cir. 2023) (Graber, J., concurring and dissenting in part)
                                                                                           5
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO            Document 36            Filed 03/11/26   Page 6 of 13




                                   1   (clarifying the Court’s statement in Morgan that the FAA’s “longstanding policy favoring

                                   2   arbitration is meant simply to place arbitration agreements on equal footing with other contracts”).

                                   3   But that does not mean the existence of an agreement should be downplayed. As I explain in

                                   4   Section I.B, supra, principles of contract interpretation still govern an arbitration clause. And if

                                   5   the terms of the contract show that enforcement of the clause is required, then the parties are

                                   6   bound by such agreement.1

                                   7          b.      Whether the Complaint is Subject to the Arbitration Provision
                                   8          Having now clarified how the FAA applies to this matter, I turn to the parties’ agreement.

                                   9   The Terms of Use provides in relevant part: “These terms limit our liability to you and generally

                                  10   require that disputes related to the Services be resolved by a dispute resolution process which may

                                  11   lead to binding arbitration.” Mot. at 9 (citing Grayson Decl., Ex. 1 (“Terms of Use”)). The

                                  12   agreement then goes on to state in pertinent part:

 United States District Court




                                  13                  22. Dispute Resolution. In the event of a dispute, claim, or
                                                      controversy arising out of or in connection with these Terms or the
                                  14                  breach, termination, enforcement, interpretation, or validity thereof
                                                      (other than for disputes, claims, or controversies related to the
                                  15                  intellectual property of a party) (collectively, “Disputes”), each
                                                      party’s senior representatives will engage in good faith negotiations
                                  16                  with the other party’s senior representatives to amicably resolve the
                                                      Dispute. If the parties are unable to resolve the Dispute within thirty
                                  17                  (30) days after the first request to engage in good faith negotiations
                                                      or within such other time period as the parties may agree to in writing,
                                  18                  then either party may commence binding arbitration under JAMS’
                                                      Comprehensive Arbitration Rules and Procedures…..Judgment on
                                  19                  the award rendered by the arbitrator may be entered in any court of
                                                      competent jurisdiction.
                                  20
                                       Id. The Arbitration Provision also contains a choice of forum clause, requiring all “arbitration
                                  21
                                       proceedings [to] take place in San Francisco, California.” Id.; Mot. at 10.
                                  22

                                  23   1
                                        It is worth noting that there is no issue of relinquishment in this case. Atelio has made it clear
                                  24   from the beginning that it sought arbitration. During the parties’ October 24, 2025 meet and
                                       confer, shortly after this suit was filed, Atelio brought the arbitration clause to NerdWallet’s
                                  25   attention, indicating it “intended to elicit consent to proceed by the way of arbitration” to avoid
                                       “unnecessary motion[s].” Mot. at 11; Declaration of Nicholas O. Kennedy (“Kennedy Decl.”)
                                  26   [Dkt. No. 20-1] ¶ 2. After their call, counsel for Atelio “followed up via e-mail four times, on
                                       November 10, November 25, and twice on December 10, to seek Plaintiff’s consent to proceed by
                                  27   way of arbitration.” Id.; Kennedy Decl. ¶¶ 4, 6, Ex. 1. Atelio’s efforts to compel arbitration were
                                  28   frequent and made early, akin to the defendant in Armstrong. 59 F.4th at 1013.

                                                                                            6
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO             Document 36         Filed 03/11/26      Page 7 of 13




                                   1           While NerdWallet does not dispute this provision exists, it argues that the agreement is

                                   2   “permissive, meaning that there was no binding arbitration agreement.” Oppo. at 3. It focuses on

                                   3   the use of the word “may” in the agreement as evidence that arbitration is permissive. Grayson

                                   4   Decl., Ex. 1 ¶ 22 (emphasis added). To support this reading, it highlights various Ninth Circuit

                                   5   and California Supreme Court cases finding that the plain meaning of “may” connotes “discretion

                                   6   or permissiveness,” unlike words such as “shall.” See Ceausu v. Progressive Cas. Ins. Co., No.

                                   7   CV 12-6254 PSG (VBKx), 2013 WL 12131280, at *7 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 10, 2013) (“The Ninth

                                   8   Circuit routinely holds that the plain meaning of the term ‘may’ connotes discretion or

                                   9   permissiveness, in contrast to ‘shall,’ the contraposition of the term, which connotes a requirement

                                  10   or duty.”); Tarrant Bell Property, LLC v. Superior Court, 51 Cal.4th 538, 542 (2011) (“[W]e

                                  11   ‘ordinarily’ construe the word ‘may’ as permissive and the word ‘shall’ as mandatory.”).

                                  12   Considering this language and caselaw together, NerdWallet urges me to conclude that the plain
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   meaning of the arbitration agreement is permissive, not mandatory. Oppo. at 5.

                                  14           Although NerdWallet touts the “plain meaning rule” as evidence of arbitration being

                                  15   permissive, it fails to consider the crucial rule of contract interpretation—reading the terms in

                                  16   context. While “the plain meaning of the term ‘may’ . . . is ordinarily understood in a permissive

                                  17   or discretionary manner,” it is “not a per se indicator of permissiveness [and] must be read in

                                  18   context.” Ceausu, 2013 WL 12131280 at *7; Kropke v. Dunbar, No. CV-16-08753-MWF

                                  19   (FFMx), 2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 236414, at *14 (C.D. Cal. Mar. 2, 2017). The Terms of Use and

                                  20   the Dispute Resolution provision, read in context, require arbitration once good faith negotiations

                                  21   fail.

                                  22           Critical to the context of the Terms of Use is that the Dispute Resolution clause is the only

                                  23   provision that discusses how a dispute can be litigated under the agreement. Only arbitration is

                                  24   mentioned as a way to resolve a dispute after good faith negotiations. There is no choice of law,

                                  25   venue or jurisdiction clause. “May” in the context of the Dispute Resolution provision gives

                                  26   permission to either party to take a formal litigation step after negotiating in good faith for thirty

                                  27   days. Parties are not required to arbitrate after that time expires—they can continue to negotiate.

                                  28   But when a party decides that negotiations will not be successful, it may take the next step
                                                                                          7
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO              Document 36         Filed 03/11/26     Page 8 of 13




                                   1   contemplated by the Terms of Use—arbitration.

                                   2             Mentor Capital, Inc. v. Bhang Chocolate Co., No. 3:14-cv-3630-LB, 2014 WL 6485666

                                   3   (N.D. Cal. Nov. 19, 2014) (Beeler, M.J.), is instructive. There, the parties disputed whether a

                                   4   similar arbitration clause was binding. That arbitration agreement read:

                                   5                    This Agreement shall be governed and construed in accordance with
                                                        the laws of the State of California.... In the event that any dispute is
                                   6                    unresolved after good faith attempts by the Parties, any Party may
                                                        demand arbitration. In that case, the matter will be submitted to final
                                   7                    and binding arbitration before an arbitrator of the American
                                                        Arbitration Association.... In the event [that] a Party brings any legal
                                   8                    action or submits any claim or controversy to arbitration with respect
                                                        to this Agreement, the prevailing Party, in addition to any other
                                   9                    remedies available to it, shall be entitled to recover reasonable
                                                        attorneys' fees and costs from the non-prevailing Party, regardless of
                                  10                    whether such action, claim or controversy is prosecuted or arbitrated
                                                        to completion.
                                  11
                                       Id. at *1 (emphasis added). The plaintiff argued that the use of the word “may” meant the
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       arbitration agreement in its entirety was permissive. Id. at *3. The Hon. Laurel Beeler disagreed,
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       finding the language “instead expresse[d] the grant of a contractual right to demand arbitration.”
                                  14
                                       Id. Judge Beeler explained in detail that “may” must be read in context:
                                  15

                                  16                    It would be artificial, and partial, to focus only on “may” when the
                                                        term is “may demand.” What can “demand” mean here if not
                                  17                    something compulsory? What would the right to “demand
                                                        arbitration” amount to if the demand were merely suggestive? (The
                                  18                    shared etymology of “demand” and “mandatory”—both words derive
                                                        from the Latin mandare, meaning “to order” or “to command”—
                                  19                    suggests something here.) Read in its still broader context, along with
                                                        the phrase “will be submitted,” the arbitration clause seems
                                  20                    inescapably mandatory. If a party demands arbitration, then, under the
                                                        arbitration clause's plain terms, “the matter will be submitted to final
                                  21                    and binding arbitration.”
                                  22   See id.

                                  23             Like the arbitration agreement in Mentor Capital, the language of Atelio and NerdWallet’s

                                  24   agreement states that either party “may commence” arbitration. See id.; Grayson Decl., Ex. 1 ¶

                                  25   22. I agree with Judge Beeler’s reasoning that it would not make sense for an agreement to

                                  26   “demand arbitration” if such a demand were “merely suggestive.” Mentor Capital, 2014 WL

                                  27   6485666, at *3. Those interpretation principles apply equally here too. The Terms of Use

                                  28   indicates that the parties “may commence binding arbitration” after “engag[ing] in good faith
                                                                                           8
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO             Document 36         Filed 03/11/26      Page 9 of 13




                                   1   negotiations.” See Grayson Decl. Ex. 1 ¶ 22. Atelio attempted to negotiate numerous times with

                                   2   NerdWallet about how to resolve their concerns. Kennedy Decl. ¶¶ 2, 4, 6. As a result, the right

                                   3   to “commence binding arbitration” was vested in Atelio, which it now seeks to enforce. That the

                                   4   word “may” is used in the agreement does not allow NerdWallet to avoid arbitration. To construe

                                   5   the agreement otherwise would be a “disfavored result under the canon that contracts should be

                                   6   construed so as to make them operative.” Id. at *4; see Health Integrated, Inc. v. Community

                                   7   Health Plan of Wash., No. C18-1522 RSM, 2019 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 15750, at *8–*9 (W.D. Wash.

                                   8   2019); Plintron Techs. USA, LLC v. Phillips, No. C24-93, 2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 65771, at *8

                                   9   (W.D. Wash. Apr. 10, 2024) (finding arbitration clauses that stated that “either Party may request

                                  10   binding arbitration” to be compulsory).

                                  11          NerdWallet points to the parties’ Technology Licensing and Onboarding Agreement

                                  12   (“TLO”) as evidence that the Terms of Use’s arbitration clause is permissive. The TLO was
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   executed around the same time as the Terms of Use and also contained an arbitration clause. That

                                  14   provision reads:
                                                      Any Dispute which cannot otherwise be resolved as provided above
                                  15                  after the parties have negotiated the resolution of the Dispute for at
                                                      least fifteen (15) business days shall be resolved by arbitration
                                  16                  conducted in accordance with the commercial arbitration rules of the
                                                      American Arbitration Association, and judgment upon the award
                                  17                  rendered by the arbitral tribunal may be entered in any court having
                                                      jurisdiction thereon.
                                  18
                                       Id.; TLO ¶ 15 (emphasis added). NerdWallet argues that because Atelio “chose to use mandatory
                                  19
                                       ‘shall’ language” in the TLO, Atelio’s use of “may” in the Terms of Use was an “intentional
                                  20
                                       choice to render arbitration permissive, not mandatory.” Oppo. at 6.
                                  21
                                              NerdWallet is mistaken. First, it has not shown why this extrinsic document should be
                                  22
                                       considered. The goal of contract interpretation is to “give effect to the mutual intention of the
                                  23
                                       parties as it existed at the time of contracting.” Mot. at 6; Int’l Bhd. of Teamsters v. NASA Servs.,
                                  24
                                       Inc., 957 F.3d 1038, 1042 (9th Cir. 2020); Cal. Civ. Code § 1636. “When a contract is reduced to
                                  25
                                       writing, the intention of the parties is to be ascertained from the writing alone, if possible.” Int’l
                                  26
                                       Bhd. of Teamsters, 957 F.3d at 1042; Cal. Civ. Code § 1639. Only when a contractual provision is
                                  27
                                       unclear should a court consider extrinsic evidence. Id. As indicated above, the language of the
                                  28
                                                                                          9
                                        Case 3:25-cv-08184-WHO           Document 36          Filed 03/11/26    Page 10 of 13




                                   1   Terms of Use is sufficiently clear in showing the arbitration clause was mandatory; it is neither

                                   2   necessary nor helpful to consider the TLO.

                                   3          The attempt to parse between a potential “may” versus “shall” distinction is unsupported

                                   4   by the caselaw cited by NerdWallet. In both its briefs and at oral argument, NerdWallet cited to

                                   5   Plintron Technologies USA, LLC v. Phillips. No. C24-93 MJP, 2024 WL 1557661 (W.D. Wash.

                                   6   Apr. 10, 2024). But Plintron shows why arbitration is mandatory here. There, the Hon. Marsha

                                   7   Pechman considered whether an arbitration clause stating that the parties “may . . . submit to

                                   8   binding arbitration” was permissive or mandatory. Id. at *1. She concluded in the context of that

                                   9   agreement that arbitration was permissive. But that agreement was different than the one at issue

                                  10   here for a number of reasons. Fundamentally, it contained a choice of law, jurisdiction, and venue

                                  11   clause, which suggested to Judge Pechman that “the parties preserved other options to resolve

                                  12   disputes, including litigation.” Id. at *2. The Terms of Use here contain no such provisions. And
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   in emphasizing the importance of context in interpreting a contract, Judge Pechman distinguished

                                  14   a case in her District, Health Integrated, Inc. v. Cmty. Health Plan of Wash., No. C18-1522 RSM,

                                  15   2019 WL 399027 (W.D. Wash. Jan. 31, 2019), that is squarely on point. The Health Integrated

                                  16   court found that “may” was mandatory in its arbitration agreement. Judge Pechman quoted the

                                  17   language from the Health Integrated agreement that she said was different from the language in

                                  18   Plintron: “if the dispute is not resolved through mediation, either Party may request binding

                                  19   arbitration.” The Health Integrated language is virtually identical to the language in our case: “If

                                  20   the parties are unable to resolve the dispute…then either party may commence binding

                                  21   arbitration…”

                                  22           Atelio’s motion to stay and compel arbitration is GRANTED. NerdWallet cannot avoid

                                  23   arbitration on the word “may” alone. Nor can it rely on other cases that parse distinctions between

                                  24   numerous contracts. Those cases are factually different. What is clear here is that both parties

                                  25   entered into an agreement that mandates arbitration for any dispute, so long as the parties (1)

                                  26   engage in good faith, (2) fail to reach an agreement, and (3) one party requests arbitration. Atelio

                                  27   has met those requirements. Accordingly, under both the FAA and canons of contract

                                   1   interpretation, I must uphold the provision and compel arbitration.2

                                   2   II.    Motion for Attorneys’ Fees
                                   3          Atelio also moves to recover attorneys’ fees for litigating this case in federal court. See

                                   4   Mot. at 21–23. It maintains that NerdWallet engaged in “bad faith [by] pursuing this frivolous

                                   5   action, in light of clear evidence that this dispute is subject to arbitration and despite FIS’ attempts

                                   6   at settling this dispute without a motion.” Id. at 21.

                                   7          District courts may award attorneys’ fees when a party has “acted in bad faith, vexatiously,

                                   8   wantonly, or for oppressive reasons.” Int’l Union of Petroleum & Indus. Workers v. W. Indus.

                                   9   Maint., Inc., 707 F.2d 425, 428 (9th Cir. 1983). Bad faith exists when “the legal and factual basis

                                  10   for the action [is] totally frivolous” or when a claim is brought with an improper purpose. B.K.B.

                                  11   v. Maui Police Dept., 276 F.3d 1091, 1108 (9th Cir. 2002), abrogated on other grounds by Fort

                                  12   Bend County, Texas v. Davis, 587 U.S. 541 (2019); see Safeco Ins. Co. of Illinois v. LSP Prods.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Grp., Inc., 659 F. Supp. 3d 1131, 1139 (D. Idaho 2023). “Courts should exercise their discretion

                                  14   to award attorney fees ‘only in exceptional cases and for dominating reasons of justice.’” Safeco,

                                  15   659 F. Supp. 3d at 1139 (quoting Beaudry Motor Co. v. Abko Props., Inc., 780 F.2d 751, 756 (9th

                                  16   Cir. 1986)).

                                  17          This is not an “exceptional case[]” where attorneys’ fees are warranted. Beaudry, 780 F.2d

                                  18   at 756. To be sure, NerdWallet incorrectly interpreted the Terms of Use. But that does not mean

                                  19   its belief was “totally frivolous.” See B.K.B., 276 F.3d at 1108. As early as July 2025, prior to

                                  20   filing suit, NerdWallet indicated to Atelio that it was “prepared to explore all available remedies,

                                  21   including the initiation of arbitration under Section 15 of [their] Technology Licensing and

                                  22   Onboarding Agreement.” Declaration of Ekumene Lysonge in Support of NerdWallet, Inc.’s

                                  23   Opposition (“Lysonge Decl.”) [Dkt. No. 30-1] Ex. 2 (July 9, 2025 correspondence between

                                  24   Ekumene Lysonge, the Chief Legal Officer at NerdWallet, and Caroline Tsai, Atelio’s Chief Legal

                                  25   and Corporate Affairs Officer)). The parties then repeatedly discussed whether the arbitration

                                  27    Atelio also makes an additional argument that the arbitration provision is both procedurally and
                                       substantively conscionable. See Mot. at 18–21. NerdWallet does not address these arguments.
                                  28   Accordingly, NerdWallet has forfeited any response to these claims, and I decline to address them
                                       here. See United States v. Caceres-Olla, 738 F.3d 1051, 1053 n.1 (9th Cir. 2013).

                                   1   provision should be understood as mandatory or permissive. Kennedy Decl. ¶¶ 4, 6. While

                                   2   NerdWallet should have been at least aware of the possibility of the arbitration clause being

                                   3   mandatory, given the language and Atelio’s interpretation of it, nothing in the record explicitly

                                   4   shows NerdWallet acted in bad faith by filing this lawsuit. I DECLINE to grant attorneys’ fees to

                                   5   Atelio.

                                   6   III.      Motions to Seal
                                   7             Atelio finally moves to seal various documents filed in support of its motions, including

                                   8   (1) a declaration from Jonathan Grayson, counsel for Atelio; (2) the Terms of Use agreement; (3)

                                   9   the TLO; and (4) the parties’ Wind-Down Plan executed on December 12, 2024. See Defendant

                                  10   Fidelity Information Services, LLC’s Administrative Motion to File Under Seal (“Sealing Mot.”)

                                  11   [Dkt. No. 19]. The justification for sealing the four documents is the same: Atelio believes each

                                  12   contains the “operative agreements governing the relationship between the parties,” which may
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   include “commercially sensitive information with respect to the terms of the parties’ relationship

                                  14   and its termination.” Id. at 2–3.

                                  15             The problem with this request is that Atelio attempts to seal these documents in their

                                  16   entirety. Much of the information contained in them, including the arbitration clause at issue and

                                  17   the TLO, have already been filed in public record or have been discussed by Atelio in its briefing.

                                  18   To request these documents be sealed in their entirety would defeat the “strong presumption in

                                  19   favor of access” and disclosure. See Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178

                                  20   (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mutual Auto. Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir.

                                  21   2003)). Nor would it make sense at this juncture, as Atelio has failed to “articulate[] compelling

                                  22   reasons supported by specific factual findings” that disclosure place them in a “competitive

                                  23   disadvantage” or would harm their “competitive and market standing” should these documents be

                                  24   public. See id. (citing San Jose Mercury News, Inc. v. U.S. Dist. Ct., 187 F.3d 1096, 1102–03 (9th

                                  25   Cir. 1999)) (emphasis added); Sealing Mot. at 4–5. Atelio’s request is therefore DENIED. Should

                                  26   Atelio seek to propose specific information that would cause competitive harm if disclosed, it may

                                  27   submit a chart that identifies its requests within ten (10) days of this Order. I will issue a final

                                  28   sealing order after reviewing the chart.
